title: Incremental solving: edit the model, re-solve

blocks.text: 4.3.4 Incremental Solving: Edit the Model, Re-Solve

Finance is preparing for a budget meeting and wants GridCap's planners ready for any outcome: what does the plan lose if 2029 is cut by 5%, by 10%, by 20%? And what if the board rules out P032, a $5,680k transmission project? Each question changes one or two numbers of a model that is otherwise the same. This lesson answers them all with one model and one solver: edit the model, re-solve, put the edit back. It also shows which edits a solver applies in place and which make MathOpt quietly start the solver over, and the two mistakes that make scenario code give wrong answers. GridCap is a fictional utility.

Lesson 2.4.3 introduced `mathopt.IncrementalSolver` on an LP and measured its warm start in simplex iterations. This lesson is about MIPs, where the solvers differ more, and about scenario code that stays correct.
The Model

The multi-period timing model of lesson 4.3.1, with the data each scenario changes marked. Its decisions are start-time variables: $`x_{i,t}= 1`$ if project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$ of its window $`T_i`$; a project starts at most once and spends its cost profile from its start year on. (Lesson 6.4.1, in section 6, builds this model step by step.)

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the years; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years of project $`i`$; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$.

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, project $`i`$'s spend in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k), **with $`B_{2029}`$ cut by a share $`s \in \{5\%, 10\%, 20\%\}`$ in the cut scenarios**.

**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$, **with $`x_{\text{P032},t} \le 0`$ for every $`t`$ in the "without P032" scenario** (an upper bound of 0, so the project cannot start).
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints**, with $`\text{spend}_y = \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t}`$:

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\sum_{i \in g} \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\text{spend}_y &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y) \quad \leftarrow (1 - s)\, B_{2029} \text{ for } y = 2029
\end{aligned}
Keep a Handle on What a Scenario Changes, and Put It Back

A scenario is an edit of the model, and an edit needs a handle on the thing it changes. That is why `plan_model.build` returns a `PlanModel` holding the start variables `x[pid, t]` and the budget rows `budget[y]` by key, not just the model. With handles, every kind of change is one call:

rows: a coefficient in a row or in the objective
delete it and add it again; it cannot be edited

blocks.text: An edit stays in the model for every solve that follows, so a scenario must put back what it changed before the next one runs. `budget_cut.py` does that with a small **context manager**, a function used in a `with` block that runs code on the way in and, thanks to `finally`, on the way out, even if the block raises an error:
`edited(row, "upper_bound", 7_000)` sets the bound for the block and restores the old one after it. It works for any attribute with a setter: a row's bounds, a variable's bounds, `integer`.
<!-- practice 1 -->
One IncrementalSolver Answers Every Scenario

`mathopt.IncrementalSolver(model, solver_type)` keeps one solver alive across solves. Each call to its `solve()` sends the solver only what changed in the model since the last call. Used as a context manager, it frees the solver when the block ends (its docstring recommends it; `close()` does the same by hand). The budget scenarios, all on one model built once:

with quiet(), mathopt.IncrementalSolver(pm.model, mathopt.SolverType.GSCIP) as solver:
    base = solver.solve(params=EXACT)
    base_plan = plan(pm, base.variable_values())

for share in (0.05, 0.10, 0.20):
    row = pm.budget[2029]
    with edited(row, "upper_bound", (1 - share) * small.budget[2029]):
        result = solver.solve(params=EXACT)
        cut_plan = plan(pm, result.variable_values())
        dropped = sorted(set(base_plan) - set(cut_plan))
        moved = sorted(p for p in cut_plan if p in base_plan and cut_plan[p] != base_plan[p])

Each cut is taken from the original budget, 8,760, because `edited` put the bound back after the scenario before. The last line checks it. The NPV falls with every deeper cut: $190k at 5%, $207k at 10%, $615k at 20%. The lists say how the plan absorbs it: a few projects dropped, more **moved** to another start year. They are one optimal plan per scenario, not the only one: where two plans tie on NPV, another solver, or another version, may return the other. That is also why the 20% plan can keep P016 while the 10% plan drops it.
Ruling out a project is a scenario too. Its start variables get an upper bound of 0 for the length of the block; `contextlib.ExitStack` enters several `edited` blocks at once and leaves them all:

with contextlib.ExitStack() as stack:
    for t in small.project("P032").starts():
        stack.enter_context(edited(pm.x["P032", t], "upper_bound", 0.0))
    result = solver.solve(params=EXACT)
    rows.append(f"without P032   NPV {result.objective_value():,.0f}")
again = solver.solve(params=EXACT)
rows.append(f"all restored   NPV {again.objective_value():,.0f}")

without P032   NPV 24,148
all restored   NPV 24,260
P032 is worth $112k of NPV to the plan, and once its bounds are back the model solves to the base NPV again: the edits left no trace.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Whether the Solver Updates in Place Depends on the Solver and the Edit

What does `IncrementalSolver.solve()` do with the changes? Its source in `solve.py` answers: it asks the solver it holds to apply them. If the solver says it cannot, MathOpt throws that solver away and builds a new one from the whole model, without telling you. Either way the result is right; what differs is whether the solver kept its copy of the model, and with it any state it could reuse.

`update_or_rebuild.py` makes six edits in a row, solving after each, and checks whether the object the `IncrementalSolver` holds is still the same one. It reads a private attribute, `_proto_solver`, so treat it as a diagnostic for learning, not as code to ship:

held = solver._proto_solver                       # private: diagnostic only
apply()
result = solver.solve()
report.append(f"{name}: {'in place' if solver._proto_solver is held else 'REBUILT'}")

GSCIP  final NPV 27,514 | budget bound: in place, objective coef: in place, new row: in place, delete row: in place, new variable: in place, integer -> continuous: REBUILT
HIGHS  final NPV 27,514 | budget bound: REBUILT, objective coef: REBUILT, new row: REBUILT, delete row: REBUILT, new variable: REBUILT, integer -> continuous: REBUILT
CP_SAT final NPV 27,514 | budget bound: REBUILT, objective coef: REBUILT, new row: REBUILT, delete row: REBUILT, new variable: REBUILT, integer -> continuous: REBUILT

items: **SCIP** applied five of the six edits in place, and rebuilt only when a variable stopped being integer.
**HiGHS and CP-SAT** rebuilt after every edit. Through MathOpt in OR-Tools 9.15, an `IncrementalSolver` on either is a fresh solve each time, the same finding lesson 2.4.3 made for HiGHS on an LP.
**All three end at the same NPV**, 27,514 (high, because the edits included deleting the 2031 budget row). A rebuild costs time, never correctness.

blocks.text: "In place" means the solver kept its model; it does not by itself mean the MIP search starts from where the last one ended. This program measures no speed, and for a MIP the gain depends on the solver and the edit. What the table does settle is the choice of tool: for many scenarios of one model, an `IncrementalSolver` is never worse than a fresh `mathopt.solve`, and on SCIP it avoids rebuilding the solver's model; on HiGHS and CP-SAT it gives nothing, and editing the model in place is still worth it, because it saves rebuilding *your* model.
Undo Every Edit, and Never Delete What a Scenario Only Switches Off
Two mistakes make scenario code quietly wrong. The first is a relative edit that is never undone:

for scenario in ("5% cut", "another 5% cut"):
    pm.budget[2029].upper_bound *= 0.95

5% cut          2029 bound 8,322.00  (budget 8,760, cut 5.00%)
another 5% cut  2029 bound 7,905.90  (budget 8,760, cut 9.75%)

The second scenario was meant to be "a 5% cut" and ran as a 9.75% one, and nothing failed. Either compute each scenario from the original data, as the loop with `edited` does with `(1 - share) * small.budget[2029]`, or restore after each scenario, and best both.
The second mistake is deleting what a scenario only needs to switch off. Deletion cannot be put back with an assignment, and every reference to a deleted variable stops working:
using a deleted variable: ValueError | no element with id 79 for element type variable

The `Variable` object still exists in Python, but the model no longer has the element it points to (id 79, the last of the 80 start variables). Deleting a variable also removes it from every row and the objective, so adding it back would mean rebuilding all of those. To take a project out of one scenario, bound its variables to 0, as the "without P032" scenario did; delete only what is gone for good. The upper bound is the one that matters: a lower bound of 1 would do the opposite and force the project in. Setting its NPV to 0 in the objective is not the same thing: the project could still start and spend budget for no value, which is a different scenario from "without". Indicator constraints are the one exception, because they cannot be edited at all (lesson 4.3.1): to change one, delete it and add a new one, and replace your handle.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **Keep a handle on what a scenario changes, and put it back.** A builder that returns rows and variables by key makes each scenario one edit; a context manager restores it even on errors.
**One IncrementalSolver answers every scenario.** Three 2029 cuts and a ruled-out project, on one model built once; the cuts cost $190k, $207k and $615k of NPV.

**Whether the solver updates in place depends on the solver and the edit.** In OR-Tools 9.15, SCIP applied bound, coefficient, row and variable edits in place; HiGHS and CP-SAT rebuilt after every edit, silently and correctly.
**Undo every edit, and never delete what a scenario only switches off.** Relative edits pile up; a deleted variable's references raise `ValueError`.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: `v.upper_bound = 0` for its start variables, then restore
bounds, objective coefficients, new and deleted rows, new variables; rebuilt on an integrality change

blocks.text: **Further reading.** OR-Tools, [MathOpt](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt): incremental solving among MathOpt's features. `IncrementalSolver` in [`solve.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/solve.py): its docstring (the `with` form, `close`, thread safety) and its `solve` method, which rebuilds the solver when an update is refused. The samples [`facility_lp_benders.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/facility_lp_benders.py), which keeps two incremental solvers through a Benders loop and edits bounds and adds rows between solves, and [`cutting_stock.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/cutting_stock.py), which re-solves a growing LP with an incremental GLOP solver.
Challenges

items: Add a fourth scenario: 2029 cut by 10% *and* P032 ruled out. Is its NPV loss the sum of the two losses alone? Predict, then run.
In `update_or_rebuild.py`, add an edit that adds an indicator constraint, and run it on SCIP. Does SCIP keep its solver?
A colleague writes `pm.budget[2029].upper_bound -= 438` for a 5% cut and `+= 438` to undo it. When could that leave the bound different from where it started?

blocks.text: Design Note: Scenarios Are Data, Edits Are Code

`budget_cut.py` lists its scenarios as numbers (`0.05, 0.10, 0.20`) and has one piece of code that turns a number into an edit and back. Adding a scenario is adding a number. The same split scales to the scenario tables planners ask for: a list of scenarios, each a set of (handle, attribute, value) edits, and one loop that applies, solves, records and restores. Section 12 builds that loop into a service.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**budget_cut.py.** The 2029 cut scenarios and the "without P032" scenario on one `IncrementalSolver`, then the two mistakes: piled-up relative edits and a deleted variable (*Keep a Handle*, *One IncrementalSolver Answers Every Scenario*, *Undo Every Edit*). *Try:* Replace the SCIP solver with HiGHS and predict whether any number in the table changes.

**update_or_rebuild.py.** Six edits on SCIP, HiGHS and CP-SAT, and whether each was applied in place (*Whether the Solver Updates in Place*). *Try:* Move the integrality edit to the front and predict what SCIP reports for the edits after it.
